CAN.mechanism: An institution with standing inside the state gets the record changed rather than the man charged: the report is rewritten, the abuser is moved to another province or another continent, and the file is the thing that disappears.
CAN.story:
Reporting a man to the police puts the institution in the file beside him; moving him does not. A transfer leaves no criminal record and hands the problem to a parish or school that has not been told, so the cost falls on the next group of children.

St John's, Newfoundland, December 1975. Detective Robert Hillier was investigating Mount Cashel Orphanage, a boys' home run by the Irish Christian Brothers, a Catholic teaching order holding privileged foster-home status from the province's social services. Two Brothers admitted molesting boys. Nine days in, the police chief and his assistant ordered Hillier to stop. References to sexual assault were removed from his report and the first version destroyed, the Justice Department had it rewritten and laid no charges, and four Brothers were moved out of the province instead. Police reopened the case in February 1989, fourteen years after the first complaint, and nine Brothers were convicted. A royal commission, a public inquiry that can compel witnesses to testify, reported in 1991 that neither the police nor the Justice Department had handled the 1975-76 files normally, and that the province's own child welfare director had insisted the Brothers be treated specially. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.

A transfer becomes permanent once it crosses a border, because a Canadian warrant has no force abroad and extradition, the handing over of a suspect by one state to another, is the receiving country's decision. Fr Eric Dejaeger, an Oblate priest in Igloolik, Nunavut, left for Belgium in 1995 as he was about to be charged; his order acknowledged knowing he was going, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses with an international warrant out for him. Returned in 2011, he was sentenced in 2015 to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children. Fr Johannes Rivoire, who left the Arctic for France in 1993, was never handed over on warrants issued in 1998 and 2022, and died there in 2024 without a trial.

Ottawa removed children itself, as policy: about 150,000 First Nations, Metis and Inuit children passed through federally funded, church-run residential schools; by the end of 2014, 37,951 claims had been filed for physical and sexual abuse. Under the settlement those claim records are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless the claimant asks to keep them.

In each of these the decision that mattered was about a document rather than a man: a report rewritten, a transfer logged as a new appointment, a claim file scheduled for destruction. When you read that an abuser was moved, allowed to resign, or died abroad before trial, ask who was told at the time, who decided not to involve police, and whether the papers will still exist when the people who were children are ready to use them.

KOR.mechanism: A state that found it cheaper to send children abroad than to support them at home, so the supply was set by foreign agencies' monthly orders and the paperwork was made to match.
KOR.story:
In March 2025 a government body in Seoul confirmed what adoptees had argued for decades. South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state commission that can take petitions from citizens and demand records from government, examined 367 people sent abroad for adoption between 1964 and 1999 to eleven countries and found human rights violations in at least 56 of those cases. Its central finding was about money: the state had used adoption abroad as a cheap alternative to paying for welfare at home.

How that worked is visible in the paperwork. Private agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet the demand of agencies in the receiving countries, so the quota came first and children had to be found to fill it. Children whose parents were known and alive were registered as orphans, because an orphan needs nobody's consent to be adopted. Consent was not properly obtained, adoptive parents were not vetted, and when a child died before the flight another child was sent out under that identity, so the file stayed correct while the person in it changed.

The pull came from the far end of the flight. About 163,898 children left between 1953 and 2008, 109,242 of them to the United States. When Seoul tried in 1974 to stop sending children to Scandinavia, Swedish, Danish and Norwegian diplomats sent nine pleas and the flights resumed; departures peaked at 8,837 in 1985. Institutions supplied the children: at Brothers Home in Busan, a state-backed facility where people labelled vagrants were confined and made to work, police brought in 3,117 of the 3,975 inmates held in 1986, and the commission counted 657 deaths there between 1975 and 1988. In February 2025 it confirmed at least 31 children had been improperly sent abroad through that one facility. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.

Where the offender was Korean, the courts kept him. US investigators traced Bitcoin payments to Welcome to Video, a Korean-run darknet site holding over 250,000 abuse videos, and 337 users were charged with leads sent to 38 countries; its operator, Son Jong-woo, served 18 months in South Korea and the Seoul High Court refused in 2020 to hand him to the United States.

An export of children needs no kidnappers if it has a monthly quota and a registration form. When an adoption programme is described as efficient, ask who set that number, who was paying at the receiving end, and what word the file used for a child whose mother was still alive.

SWE.mechanism: The receiving end of an adoption pipeline is what keeps it running: Swedish demand, pressed by Swedish diplomats, kept children coming from countries where they were bought, relabelled or taken.
SWE.story:
In January 1975 Sweden's ambassador in Seoul asked the South Korean government to keep sending children. South Korea had just tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia; Swedish, Danish and Norwegian diplomats together sent nine such pleas, and the flights resumed. Between 1957 and 2005 Sweden received 9,051 Korean children.

That is the part of intercountry adoption that is easy to miss. The sending country supplies children, but the demand that sets the number sits in the receiving country, where agencies have waiting families and fees to collect. South Korea's own Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with living parents as orphans, which is the paperwork a quota requires.

Korea was one source among several. In Chile, children were taken from mostly poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and placed with families in the United States and Europe, Sweden included; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship, and a Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad between 1970 and 1999. In Sri Lanka in the 1980s, babies were bought or taken from hospitals and handed to paid women who posed as the birth mothers in court, with children going to the Netherlands, Britain, Germany and Sweden. Greek-born children, many of them labelled orphans after the civil war or born outside marriage, were adopted into Sweden, the Netherlands and the United States between 1950 and 1975 under procedures conducted quickly and in secrecy.

Adoptees from Chile pressed Sweden to examine its own part, and it did. An independent state inquiry reported on 2 June 2025 in nearly 1,600 pages, covering 65 years of adoptions and documenting irregularities and illegalities that Swedish authorities had some knowledge of at the time. Sweden had already stopped taking children from South Korea in 2024.

Sweden appears at the receiving end of the online trade as well, in the plainest way: commercial web hosting. Abuse material has to sit on a server someone rents, and the Internet Watch Foundation, a British organisation that finds such material and has it taken down, acted on 6,820 web addresses hosted in Sweden in 2025, two per cent of its total.

A receiving country looks like the safe end of an adoption, the place where a child arrives. The useful questions are what its officials knew about how the child was obtained, when they knew it, and whether they used their position to slow the traffic or to keep it moving.

MEX.mechanism: The cost of exposure is shifted onto the person who reports: the journalist is arrested, the seminarians' letters go unanswered, and almost no complaint survives the journey from prosecutor's file to sentence.
MEX.story:
In 2005 the journalist Lydia Cacho published Los demonios del Eden, which described the Cancun hotel businessman Jean Succar Kuri as the head of a child-exploitation network and linked it to a Puebla businessman, Kamel Nacif, and to Puebla's state governor, Mario Marin. What happened next was aimed at her. Police from Puebla arrested Cacho in Cancun and drove her about 900 miles across the country to Puebla; she says she was tortured. Leaked recordings published in February 2006 captured Nacif and Marin discussing her jailing as a favour and having her abused in jail. In November 2007 Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6-4 that Marin had no case to answer. Succar Kuri was convicted in 2011 and died in custody in 2024. Marin was arrested in 2021, not over the abuse but over Cacho's alleged torture, and his trial continues; neither he nor Nacif has been convicted.

Complaints made quietly fared no better. A former seminarian wrote to the Vatican in 1976 about Marcial Maciel, the Mexican priest who founded the Legion of Christ, a wealthy religious order. More letters followed in 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998. Nothing happened until 2006, thirty years after the first letter, when the Vatican told Maciel to retire to prayer and penitence; he was never tried or removed from the priesthood. The order's own report in 2019 found 33 of its priests had abused 175 minors since 1941, at least 60 of them by Maciel.

The attrition is measurable. In January 2020 the Mexican bishops' conference said it had investigated 426 priests over ten years and removed 217 from their duties, which costs a man his job and is not a criminal case. El Universal reported the following month that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into sexual offences against minors by religious figures between 2009 and 2019, and that four prosecutors' offices recorded six sentences.

Children the state placed itself were not outside this. Fourteen children went missing in February 2009 from Casitas del Sur, a private church-run shelter in Mexico City where city prosecutors had placed children, and a city legislator accused prosecutors' staff of warning the shelter before searches so children could be moved. At La Gran Familia in Zamora, more than 40 parents' complaints had reached state and federal authorities before a 2014 raid freed 432 children and 138 adults.

Mexico shows what happens where reporting carries a higher personal risk than offending. Count the complaints that existed before anything was done, find out which office received them, and ask what became of the people who filed them.

BEL.mechanism: Every fact needed to stop the man was already in a government file; the failure was in the handling of it, and the unproven part of the story became the famous part.
BEL.story:
In 1992 Marc Dutroux was released early from a 13.5-year sentence for rape, over the objections of a prosecutor and a psychiatrist who had assessed him. Parole decisions like that turn on a prediction about a man's future, and the officials who make them do not meet the children who are affected if the prediction is wrong. In 1995 and 1996 Dutroux kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19. He was found guilty of kidnapping and raping all six, of killing two, and of causing the deaths of two others.

What the Belgian record shows is not a secret network but the handling of information the state already had. His own mother wrote to the authorities in 1995 that he was holding two girls. Police treated him as a prime suspect from June 1995 and took 14 months to arrest him. Officers searching his house heard voices in the cellar and left; videotapes seized from him were not reviewed. Two separate national forces, the Gendarmerie and the judicial police, were working the case in competition rather than together, so what one knew the other did not act on. When the investigating judge was removed in October 1996 for attending a fundraising dinner for victims, hundreds of thousands of people walked through Brussels in the White March. A parliamentary inquiry criticised the investigation, Belgium later reorganised its police, and in 2004 Dutroux was given a life sentence, his ex-wife Michelle Martin 30 years and Michel Lelievre 25.

Alongside this ran a separate story. Witnesses told investigators in 1996 and 1997 of abuse parties involving Dutroux and prominent people. Prosecutors dismissed the statements, investigators were criticised for leading one key witness, and an officer charged in 1997 with falsifying her statements was cleared in 1999. Those claims of an elite network have never been established.

The church side of the Belgian record was decided by a legal deadline. A church commission set up in 2000 received 33 formal complaints and upheld 32 of them, but most were time-barred, meaning the period in which a prosecution could legally be brought had expired, so an upheld complaint produced no case. A second commission received 475 complaints in six months in 2010 and linked 13 suicides to clerical abuse.

Nothing in the Dutroux file required new information to act on; it required someone to read what was there and own the decision. When a country announces reforms after a case like this, the test is whether letters, tapes and tip-offs now reach a single office that must answer for them, not whether a new agency has been named.

COL.mechanism: A country with no national inquiry does not get a smaller problem, only a smaller record: Colombia's counts are produced by a foreign inquiry, a UN verification team, a US report and a journalist who had to win a court order.
COL.story:
In August 2020 Colombia's Constitutional Court ordered the Archdiocese of Medellin to hand over its files on 915 cases of accused clergy to the journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos within 48 hours. The files were not fully produced. That order exists because Colombia has had no national inquiry into institutional abuse: no government-appointed body with the power to compel evidence, hear survivors and publish a total. Without one, a church keeps its own records and decides what leaves the building, and a reporter has to go to court for the records.

What a count looks like when someone does have that power can be seen in the war cases. The Special Jurisdiction for Peace, the court created by the 2016 peace agreement to try crimes committed during the conflict, opened a case on the recruitment and use of children by the former FARC-EP guerrillas. By August 2021 it had identified 18,677 victims provisionally and formally accredited 9,854 of them as participants in the case. It has indicted former commanders for war crimes including child recruitment and sexual violence, and former FARC secretariat members have acknowledged responsibility. Current violence is counted by UN staff who verify incidents one by one: 33 girls subjected to sexual violence in 2024, by the ELN, FARC dissident groups and the Clan del Golfo, and 26 cases in 2023, two of them by Colombia's own armed forces. A verified figure is a floor, not a total.

The adoption record was written abroad. In 1981 the New York Times reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a multimillion-dollar ring in which hundreds of poor Andean children were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad with forged papers. Adoption abroad continued, with 20,864 children sent between 2003 and 2022. The official finding of wrongdoing came from the Netherlands, whose 2021 state inquiry found serious violations in adoptions from several countries including Colombia between 1967 and 1998, and found that Dutch officials had known for years and not intervened.

Present-day trafficking is described mainly in the US State Department's yearly report, which places sex-trafficking networks run by Tren de Aragua and the ELN on the Venezuelan border, moving victims out through the transport hub at Cucuta, and describes recruitment of Colombian and displaced Venezuelan girls into webcam studios. It also records two complicit officials given plea deals of 7.5 years, below the statutory minimum, the lowest sentence the law allows for the offence.

The thinness of a country's record can be a fact about its institutions rather than about its children. When a map or a report shows few cases somewhere, ask who in that country is required to count, what powers they have to demand documents, and whether anyone has ever used them.

VNM.mechanism: A child with living parents becomes adoptable by being written down as abandoned, so demand abroad is met by changing documents rather than by finding orphans.
VNM.story:
In April 1975, as South Vietnam was falling, President Ford directed that $2 million of a special foreign aid fund be used to fly 2,000 South Vietnamese orphans to the United States. More than 3,300 children were flown out, some to Australia. The first flight, a C-5 cargo plane, crash-landed shortly after take-off on 4 April, killing many of the children aboard. A lawsuit against the federal government and the adoption agencies argued that many of the children were not orphans at all: poor families sometimes placed a child in an orphanage to keep the child fed without intending to give the child up, and many of the adoption records carried no parental consent.

The same gap between a child's situation and a child's paperwork reappeared in peacetime, and it can be followed through one word. An adoption abroad needs a child who is legally free, which usually means abandoned or orphaned, so the number of children recorded as abandoned is the supply. The United States issued 7,498 immigrant visas to children adopted from Hanoi between 1994 and 2014, peaking at 828 in 2007. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi reported that the number of babies recorded as deserted had risen seventeenfold or more at orphanages in seven provinces. Vietnam did not renew the adoption agreement with the United States when it expired that September. In 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people for abuse of power: the head of two provincial social welfare centres and doctors and nurses at village clinics, accused of soliciting infants from poor families and falsifying documents that said the babies had been abandoned. Through that one route, 266 babies were sent abroad between 2005 and July 2008.

Children also left for other buyers. Most of the children in the brothels of Svay Pak, across the border in Cambodia, were ethnic Vietnamese, many sold by destitute families, and Hmong and other ethnic-minority girls are lured or abducted into China for forced marriage. Offenders arrived from the other direction. After his 1999 conviction in Britain, the singer Paul Gadd, known as Gary Glitter, was expelled from Cambodia, moved to Vietnam and was convicted there in 2006 of obscene acts with girls aged 10 and 11. In 2007, the year an Australian organisation documented 80 commercial cases of exploitation of children by foreigners in Sa Pa, Vietnam put a child sex tourism unit inside its police ministry.

A sudden rise in abandoned babies is not a social trend; it is a clerical one, and somebody signs each form. When a sending country is praised for the number of children it places, ask who certifies that a child has no parents, who pays that person, and what happens to the certificate afterwards.

ZWE.mechanism: Zimbabwe is the receiving end of other countries' decisions: an English trust solved its problem by sending a man there and telling nobody, and Britain had earlier sent children into a school where their complaints were punished.
ZWE.story:
An institution that moves an abuser abroad is relying on something simple: nobody is required to tell the destination. In 1982 an internal report written for the Iwerne Trust, which ran evangelical Christian camps for boys in England, described how its former chairman, the barrister John Smyth, had beaten boys and young men he met through those camps. The men who received that report did not take it to the police, who were not told until 2013.

In 1984 Smyth moved to Zimbabwe, and in 1986 he founded Zambesi Ministries, which ran camps for boys there. A 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992. Smyth was arrested in 1997 and was never charged in any country. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001, where a later review found it highly likely his abuse continued until his death in Cape Town in 2018. That review, by Keith Makin, was published on 7 November 2024; it found an active cover-up in England, described Smyth as a problem solved and exported to Africa, and found no evidence that anyone had tried to warn the Zimbabwean authorities. The Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby, resigned five days later.

Britain had used the same country as a destination for children. Between 1946 and 1956, 276 British child migrants were sent to the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College. England's national inquiry into child sexual abuse found that children who told the headmaster a padre had sexually abused them were beaten and warned against spreading malicious lies, and could not determine whether the Fairbridge Society in Britain knew of the allegations. Its 2018 report called the migration schemes a deeply flawed government policy.

For what is happening now, the available account comes from the US State Department's annual trafficking report, which has no power to compel evidence in Zimbabwe and relies on what embassies and organisations there can see. It describes women and children exploited in sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines, sometimes in exchange for money or food, and children used as panners and couriers carrying ore. It notes practices that put girls within reach: families trading a daughter for food or money, and ngozi, in which a relative is given to another family to atone for a killing. It records continuing low-level complicity by officials.

Exporting an abuser ends the problem for the institution that exports him and begins it for children who have never heard of that institution. When you read that a man was sent overseas, moved on, or quietly left a post, ask who in the sending country had the duty to warn the receiving one, and what they were protecting by staying quiet.

AFG.mechanism: When the men abusing children are a government's useful allies, or the government itself, the rules meant to force a response contain an exception, and the exception is the thing that gets used.
AFG.story:
In 2011 a US Army captain, Dan Quinn, and a sergeant, Charles Martland, beat an Afghan Local Police commander who had admitted chaining up and raping a 12-year-old boy. Quinn was relieved of his command and Martland was at first separated from the army. The commander led a militia the United States was arming and paying to hold ground, and the practice he took part in has a name in Afghanistan, bacha bazi: boys kept and abused by commanders.

In September 2015 the New York Times reported that American soldiers had been told to ignore such abuse by Afghan allies, in some cases even when it happened on US bases. The reason was the alliance: a commander who holds a district is hard to replace, and a complaint that removes him costs the war effort something immediate, while the boy costs it nothing. There was a law meant to prevent this trade-off. The Leahy Law bars US military aid to foreign units credibly found to have committed gross human rights violations, so that American money cannot fund them. Nearly 100 members of Congress asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction, an official auditor reporting to Congress, to look into it. His report, made public in January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces committed between 2010 and 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and concluded that the full extent of child sexual assault by those forces may never be known. The Pentagon used the law's notwithstanding exception, a clause allowing aid to continue anyway, including an approval in December 2015 of continued funding for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.

After the Taliban took power the accused became the state. UN staff verified sexual violence against 12 children in Afghanistan in 2023, ten of those cases attributed to the Taliban, along with the abduction of three children for that purpose, and verified six cases in 2024. Verification means a UN team could confirm each incident, which in a country whose authorities are the subject of the report is a floor far below the real number. In 2024 boys aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run religious schools told the broadcaster Radio Azadi that teachers pressured them and their classmates into sexual acts. One 16-year-old said he reported a teacher to the man in charge of the school, who told the teacher to stop; the teacher admitted it and continued. A UN report counted 6,836 Taliban-established madrasahs for boys.

Afghanistan is about where a complaint can go. A reporting rule written into law lasts only as long as its exceptions allow, and when the school, the militia and the government are one authority, a boy's complaint ends with the man he complained about. When an official calls abuse a matter for local authorities, ask who those authorities answer to.

MDA.mechanism: Moldova supplies the children and women; the buyers were international personnel who were flown home instead of charged, which removed both the defendants and the witnesses.
MDA.story:
Through the late 1990s, girls and women from Moldova were sold to bar owners in post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage, meaning they were told they owed the cost of their transport and papers and had to work it off, which keeps a person in place without locks. Human Rights Watch documented this in 2002 and found local Bosnian police among the owners, the guards and the customers.

The buyers also included the people sent to fix the country. Eighteen monitors of the UN International Police Task Force, police officers seconded from other countries to supervise Bosnia's own, bought women, used brothels or faced trafficking-related charges; all were sent home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. Repatriation ends a case twice over: the man is beyond the reach of the courts where the offence happened, his own country rarely takes it up, and he is no longer available to testify about anyone else. A US Army investigation documented contractors from the firm DynCorp buying women; one confessed to buying a woman, along with an Uzi, for 1,600 Deutschmarks. DynCorp dismissed Kathryn Bolkovac, the monitor who reported the trafficking, and a British tribunal found in August 2002 that the dismissal was unfair.

In Kosovo the same arrangement scaled up. Amnesty International reported in 2004 that the arrival of NATO troops and UN administrators in 1999 had made Kosovo a destination for trafficked women and girls, with the international presence generating 80 per cent of traffickers' income; the women came mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia. The UN's peacekeeping department acknowledged that year that peacekeepers had come to be seen as part of the problem rather than the solution, and Amnesty found no criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

Who gets taken from Moldova is not random. The US State Department reported in 2007 that women and children were being trafficked out to Russia, Turkey, Israel and the United Arab Emirates. UNICEF found that children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more likely to be trafficked than other children, because a child who ages out of state care has no family making enquiries, no address and no income. The 2025 US report describes the same children being approached now through social media, video chat and fake job advertisements, with abuse images used as a grooming tool. Moldovan courts convicted 33 traffickers in 2024, 22 of them for sex trafficking, and a former police officer was convicted of labour trafficking and given 20 years.

Moldova shows demand arriving in uniform, and a transfer order doing the work of an acquittal. When an institution answers abuse by its own staff with a flight home, ask which court has lost the case, and who else that man could have been made to name.

VAT.mechanism: The Holy See is both a church and a sovereign state, so it can pull an accused man out of the country where the children are, decline to hand him over, and hold the only trial itself.
VAT.story:
A nuncio is the Vatican's ambassador to a country. Like other ambassadors he cannot normally be prosecuted by the state he is posted to, and the government that sent him can order him home at any time without explaining why.

In August 2013 the Holy See recalled Archbishop Jozef Wesolowski, its nuncio to the Dominican Republic since 2008, amid allegations that he had abused minors. Dominican prosecutors opened their criminal investigation on 4 September, by which time he was inside Vatican City. The Holy See told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition, the formal handing over of a suspect to another state. A church tribunal found him guilty and he was laicised, stripped of the priesthood, in June 2014. A Vatican prosecutor indicted him in June 2015 for abusing children in the Dominican Republic between 2008 and 2013 and for possessing abuse images. He was found dead in his Vatican rooms that August, before the trial. A Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, Fr Wojciech Gil, shows the other route: he went back to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic, and a Polish court tried him there and sentenced him in March 2015 to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

The arrangement held in other postings. Monsignor Carlo Capella was recalled from the Holy See's embassy in Washington in 2017 over abuse images; the Vatican's own tribunal convicted him in June 2018 and gave him five years and a 5,000 euro fine, and he was not tried in the United States or Canada. France took a different course with Archbishop Luigi Ventura, the nuncio there: a Paris court tried him in his absence and convicted him in December 2020, with an eight-month suspended sentence.

Rome also took men in. Fr Bernard Prince was appointed to a post in Rome in 1991, and a 1993 church letter discussed keeping him hidden in the Vatican rather than letting him face justice in Canada. Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Oran resigned in 2017 after complaints from his clergy and was given a job at the Vatican's patrimony office that December; Argentina convicted him in 2022 of abusing two adult seminarians. Documents stayed behind the same wall: when Ireland's Murphy Commission asked the Holy See for files in 2009, none were supplied, and an inquiry without documents can only record what witnesses still remember.

Sovereignty is the mechanism here, not secrecy. When a church official accused abroad is recalled, suspended or given a post at headquarters, the questions are which prosecutor has lost access to him, whether the country where the children live ever asked for him, and what answer it got.

IDN.mechanism: A document does the work: a forged household registration turns a sold baby into a family member, and a marriage contract turns the purchase of a nine-year-old into a private arrangement nobody has to police.
IDN.story:
In July 2025 police in West Java said a group had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, for 11 to 16 million rupiah each. Some had been reserved while still in the womb. What made the sales workable was not stealth but paperwork: the group prepared false family cards and passports in Pontianak. A family card is the household registration document that records who belongs to a family, so a forged one gives a bought baby a lawful identity and makes the crossing a routine trip with a child who is, on paper, a relative. Thirteen people were arrested, six babies about to be moved were taken into protection, and police asked Interpol for help tracing the adopters, who are in another country and were not accused of anything by those police.

The legal version of the same trade has a longer history, and the finding about it came from the receiving end. A Dutch government inquiry reported in February 2021 that there had been serious violations in intercountry adoptions from several countries including Indonesia between 1967 and 1998, and that Dutch officials had known of wrongdoing for years without intervening. The Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption immediately.

The second document is a marriage certificate. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says tourists from the Middle East pay more than 700 dollars for week-long contract marriages in Puncak, in Bogor, involving girls as young as nine, and that the government tacitly accepted the practice. A marriage, even one lasting a week, reclassifies the man from a buyer into a husband and the girl from a child being sold into a wife, which takes the transaction out of the reach of anyone whose job is to stop the sale of children. The report also describes exploitation of children by foreign offenders as prevalent in the Riau Islands, the chain that sits across the water from Singapore and is reached by ferry, with women and girls coerced into commercial sex in Batam, where police arrested a Singaporean man in October 2017 accused of molesting three boys. It records corruption and official complicity as significant obstacles to any of this being stopped.

Indonesia shows the paperwork stage of the trade, where the risky part is not moving a child but registering one. When you read that children were sold or married off somewhere, ask which office issues the document that made it legal-looking, what it costs to obtain, and whether anyone has ever been prosecuted for signing one.

PRT.mechanism: Children in the state's own care were abused by men whose standing outweighed every complaint, and the twenty-seven-year delay was produced inside the institutions that received those complaints.
PRT.story:
In 1975 a teacher at Casa Pia, a Portuguese state institution that cared for about 4,500 children in Lisbon, began reporting the abuse of boys to the institution's leaders and to the police. In 1981 police accused a caretaker. Neither step led to any legal action. A complaint only travels as far as the person who receives it is willing to take it, and these children were wards of the state, so there were no parents behind them to keep asking. One of the men eventually convicted, the diplomat Jorge Ritto, had been removed as consul in Stuttgart around 1969 to 1971 after a complaint about an under-age boy, and remained in the diplomatic service afterwards.

The case became public in 2002, twenty-seven years after the teacher's first report. A trial opened in 2004 and ended on 3 September 2010 with six of the seven defendants convicted. Carlos Silvino, a former Casa Pia driver, confessed to 639 charges of abusing boys or procuring them for others and was given 18 years. Procuring is the hinge of a case like this: a low-ranking employee with keys, a van and the children's trust can supply men who never come near the building. Those men were the television presenter Carlos Cruz and the doctor Joao Ferreira Diniz, seven years each, Ritto, six years and eight months, the lawyer Hugo Marcal, six years and two months, and Casa Pia's former governor Manuel Abrantes, five years and nine months. All of them except Silvino denied the charges. A woman accused of letting her house be used was acquitted, and a former government minister, Paulo Pedroso, was detained during the investigation but never tried.

The Catholic Church in Portugal counted itself much later and under its own control. A commission set up by the bishops and led by the child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht reported on 13 February 2023, after hearing more than 500 survivors, that at least 4,815 children had been abused in the church since 1950. Most of the offences were time-barred, meaning the legal period for bringing a prosecution had expired, so the commission passed 25 cases to prosecutors. An inquiry can produce a national total and almost no cases at the same time.

Portugal shows how long a complaint can sit when the people accused have professional standing and the children have none. When an institution says it has no record of earlier warnings, ask who was in charge in the years the abuse is now said to have started, and whether any of them is still deciding what happens to complaints.

GAB.mechanism: A UN mission cannot prosecute its own soldiers, so when Gabonese troops were accused the only available step was to fly them home to the government that sent them.
GAB.story:
Soldiers serving in a United Nations peacekeeping mission remain under the criminal law of their own country. The UN can take statements, suspend payments and send a contingent home, but it cannot charge anyone; only the government that supplied the troops can do that. This is the single fact that decides what happens next in almost every case of abuse by peacekeepers.

In 2014 and 2015, in the town of Dekoa in the Central African Republic, troops from Gabon and Burundi were serving in MINUSCA, the UN mission sent to protect civilians there. The Secretary-General's 2017 report records two allegations concerning Dekoa and personnel from those two countries, which led investigators to interview some 136 alleged victims. Those two allegations accounted for 48 per cent of all the victims the UN recorded across all its missions in 2016. The report states that the investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and that 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges.

The allegations continued. On 15 September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in the mission, about 450 personnel, would be repatriated after further allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse, and Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report links most of the mission's allegations involving multiple victims in 2021 to a single troop-contributing country repatriated that September.

What happens inside Gabon itself is largely unmeasured. The 2026 update of the Childlight research programme, which pools representative population surveys to estimate how many children are exploited online, found no such surveys for West and Central Africa, so for that part of the problem there is no figure for Gabon at all, which is different from there being none of it.

Repatriation solves the mission's problem and transfers the case to the one authority with no incentive to pursue it. When a contingent is sent home over abuse, the question is not whether the UN acted but what its home government did after the plane landed: whether charges were brought, in which court, and whether the children in Dekoa were ever told.

MOZ.mechanism: Armed men with money arriving in a wrecked economy produce a market in children within months, and in Mozambique the men have included peacekeepers, insurgents and the country's own soldiers and police.
MOZ.story:
Mozambique's civil war ended with a peace treaty in 1992, and the United Nations sent a mission, ONUMOZ, to oversee the transition. A UN study on the impact of armed conflict on children, led by Graca Machel and published in August 1996, found that ONUMOZ soldiers had recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. The study looked at twelve countries and found that in six of them the arrival of peacekeeping troops was followed by a rapid rise in child prostitution.

That is a pattern rather than a coincidence. A mission arrives in a place where the economy has stopped, bringing thousands of men on foreign salaries into towns where families have lost their fields and their relatives. Girls are the cheapest thing on sale, the soldiers are paid in cash and leave on rotation, and nobody local has the standing to complain to a foreign army.

Thirty years later the war in the north put children in the hands of a different group of armed men. In Cabo Delgado province, UN staff verified the abduction of 468 children in 2024, 371 boys and 97 girls, with 392 of the abductions carried out to recruit them, along with sexual violence against five girls. In 2023 they verified 92 abductions and sexual violence against twelve girls. Verification means that UN staff were able to confirm each individual case, so these are the incidents that could be documented, not an estimate of the total.

The 2023 figures also name the perpetrators, and they were not only the insurgents. Of those twelve cases of sexual violence against girls, five were attributed to Mozambique's own Defence Armed Forces, four to armed groups and three to the police Rapid Intervention Unit.

Mozambique teaches that the uniform tells you nothing about which side of this a man is on: peacekeepers in the 1990s, an insurgency now, and the national army and police in the same report as the insurgents. When a government promises to protect children in a conflict zone by sending more troops or police, ask who counts the cases involving those forces, and to whom they report it.

SLE.mechanism: Consent was the thing taken: parents handed children over for a medical check and an American court turned that into a permanent adoption, which no Sierra Leonean parent had the standing to undo.
SLE.story:
In 1998, during Sierra Leone's civil war, about 29 children staying at a centre in Makeni run by a group called Help A Needy Child International were taken to Freetown for what their parents understood to be medical checks. The children did not come back. Their parents learned later that they had been adopted by families in the United States.

An adoption abroad is lawful only if the parents gave up the child knowingly, and that consent is the one part of the process that happens in a village, in a local language, often with a signature on a form the family cannot read. Everything after it happens in another country: the visa, the court order, the new birth certificate. Once a US court has granted an adoption, the parents' rights are gone, and a family in Makeni has no way to appear before that court, no lawyer and no money to travel. The paperwork is sound at every later stage because the flaw is at the start.

The route stayed open for years. Between 1994 and 2014 the United States issued 385 immigrant visas to children adopted from Sierra Leone, with a peak of 56 in 2003. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012, fourteen years after the Makeni children were taken, a presidential commission shut the organisation down and concluded that the biological families cannot be said to have genuinely consented. The finding named the wrong but did not return the children.

What is happening to children in Sierra Leone now is largely unrecorded. The Childlight research programme, which estimates online exploitation of children from representative national surveys, found in 2026 that no such survey exists anywhere in West or Central Africa, so there is no figure for this country.

A child can be taken with a signature rather than by force. When an adoption programme is described as rescuing children from a war, ask who explained the papers to the parents, in what language, and what the parents were told they were agreeing to.

WSM.mechanism: Parents were promised schooling and signed documents that ended their parenthood, and when the agency was caught the charges were reduced to immigration offences that carried no prison.
WSM.story:
Between 2002 and 2005 a Utah adoption agency called Focus on Children, run by Scott and Karen Banks, worked in Samoa. Parents were told their children would go to the United States for a period to attend school. About 80 children went, and they were adopted permanently.

The gap between those two sentences is the whole mechanism. A family agreeing to send a child away to study expects letters, visits and a return. An adoption order made by an American court ends the parents' legal relationship with the child for good, and it cannot be reversed from Samoa. Distance did the rest: the families could not telephone the new household, could not read the court file, and had no official in either country whose job was to check that the promise and the paperwork matched.

In February 2007 a federal indictment charged the Banks couple and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. On 6 January 2009 all of them pleaded guilty to misdemeanour counts of aiding the improper entry of a foreigner, and the agency pleaded guilty to a felony conspiracy. In a plea agreement the prosecution drops the serious charges in exchange for admissions to lesser ones, which ends the case without a trial and without any court ruling on what was done to the children. In February 2009 the judge sentenced them to five years of probation and barred them from adoption work. None of them went to prison, and the offences they admitted were about immigration documents rather than about children.

Samoa has also been used as a destination for an abuser. A Salesian priest convicted of abuse in Melbourne, Australia, was allegedly moved to Samoa to avoid further police investigation; that remains an allegation.

Samoa shows a case where everybody involved kept their liberty and the children stayed where they had been sent. When an agency is prosecuted over an adoption programme, read what it finally pleaded guilty to, because the charge that sticks tells you what the system was willing to treat as the offence.

GRL.mechanism: A government removed children in order to change what they would become, selected them through the adults the families trusted, and settled with the survivors seventy years later only after they sued.
GRL.story:
In May 1951 Danish authorities asked teachers and priests in Greenland to identify children between six and ten years old. Twenty-two Inuit children were then sent to foster families in Denmark to be brought up as what the plan called little Danes. Save the Children Denmark took part in organising it. Many of the families were reluctant to let their children go.

The choice of who did the selecting is the part worth understanding. A government that regards a people's language and household as the obstacle to their children's future does not need force if it asks the teacher and the priest to point out the promising ones, because those are the people a parent is least able to refuse and most likely to believe. The children were not being taken from danger. They were being taken to be made into something else, and the Danish state said so.

About a year and a half later, 16 of them returned to Greenland, but they were not sent home. They were placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross, and many never lived with their families again. The other six were adopted by Danish families and stayed.

A report in 2020 found that half of the 22 later had mental health problems. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, nearly seventy years after the experiment. In March 2022, after the survivors took legal action, the six who were still alive were each awarded 250,000 kroner. Compensation arrived only because people sued, and by then there were six of them to pay.

This was not a secret operation; it was published policy carried out with the help of children's charities and described as being for the children's benefit. When a state proposes to remove children for their own good, ask who draws up the list of children, what a family is allowed to say in response, and how many of them will still be alive when the apology comes.

URY.mechanism: State agents took a newborn and gave her a false identity, and the country then passed a law that made the crime unexaminable until an international court ruled the law could not apply.
URY.story:
A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine woman was detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 and moved secretly across the river to Montevideo. The transfer was possible because of Operation Condor, an arrangement among South American military governments to hold and hand over each other's opponents, which let a person disappear from one country's records and never appear in another's. She gave birth in a military hospital in Uruguay. In December 1976 the baby was taken from her and left with a police officer's family, who raised the girl under another name for 23 years. The mother was never seen again.

Taking the child was not incidental to the disappearance; it completed it. A baby raised under a new name by a family loyal to the service that took her leaves no one to ask where her mother went.

In 1986 Uruguay passed the Expiry Law, an amnesty covering crimes committed under military rule. An amnesty does not say an act was lawful; it removes the state's power to prosecute it, so a prosecutor who finds evidence has nowhere to take it. That law was used to close the investigation into this case in 2003.

On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, a regional court whose judgments bind the states that accept its authority, found Uruguay responsible for the mother's enforced disappearance and for the suppression of the daughter's identity, and ruled that the Expiry Law had no legal effect in the case. The law had stood for 25 years; it took a court outside the country to set it aside.

Uruguay shows that the most effective cover-up can be a statute. When a government offers an amnesty, a reconciliation law or a sealing of old files, ask what happens to a child whose identity was changed under cover of it, and which court is left with the power to look.

SLV.mechanism: Children taken by the army during a war were passed into foreign adoptions, and because the military has never opened its archives the searching is done by relatives and a private organisation instead of the state.
SLV.story:
In 1982, during El Salvador's civil war, the army carried out an operation known as the Guinda de Mayo. Two young sisters of the Serrano Cruz family disappeared during it. In 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, a regional court whose rulings bind the states that accept its authority, gave judgment on their case.

They were two among many. Pro-Busqueda, an organisation founded in 1994 to search for children who went missing in the war, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared, mostly taken by the armed forces. Many of them were adopted through flawed procedures into families in the United States, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands.

The route from a military operation to a foreign adoption runs through a document. A child picked up during a sweep arrives at an institution without a name or a surviving parent to claim one, and once the child is recorded as abandoned, the adoption that follows is lawful on its face in the receiving country. The adoptive families, in most cases, were told nothing.

That makes the military's own records the only place where the beginning of each story is written: which unit was in which village on which day, and what was done with the children found there. The armed forces have not granted access to those archives despite years of requests. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010, but a commission without the files is dependent on memory, bones and volunteered DNA.

The result is that the state which took the children is not the body looking for them. El Salvador teaches that in these cases the crime and the evidence are held by the same institution. When a government sets up a search body, ask whether it has the legal power to demand military archives, and whether anyone has tested that power in court.

ALB.mechanism: Albania's children are counted abroad and prosecuted at home, and the two numbers do not meet: thousands of referrals in Britain against four trafficking convictions in a year.
ALB.story:
Britain runs a system called the National Referral Mechanism, in which police, councils and charities refer anyone they believe has been trafficked so the government can decide whether to recognise them as a victim. In 2024 Albanians were the second most common nationality referred, 2,492 people, though 95 per cent of them were referred as adults. That is a count made by the country where people arrive, which is the usual way this gets measured, and it says nothing about who recruited them or where.

At the other end, the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report describes what happens inside Albania. Traffickers exploit Albanian women and children in sex trafficking and forced labour, with the pressure rising in the tourist season, when the coast fills with visitors and short-term cash work appears for a few months. Roma and Balkan-Egyptian children are forced to beg. Albanians who migrate to Western Europe, Britain especially, are vulnerable to being forced into crime, which matters for how they are treated when found: a child caught growing cannabis or selling drugs looks to the police like an offender first.

Against that, the report records that Albanian courts convicted two sex traffickers and two labour traffickers, the first trafficking convictions in the country since 2021. A conviction in these cases needs a victim willing to give evidence against someone who knows their family and village, and often the trafficker is a relative, so most cases never reach that point.

Albania shows the gap between where victims are identified and where traffickers are tried. When a country's trafficking figures look small, check whether those numbers come from its own courts or from the arrival countries' paperwork, because the two are counting different people at different stages.

TZA.mechanism: The exploitation is arranged inside relationships that look ordinary, by brokers and foster families moving girls from the mainland to Zanzibar, and the only account of it is written by a foreign government.
TZA.story:
Girls and women from mainland Tanzania are recruited to Zanzibar with false promises, according to the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report, and are then exploited in commercial sex, forced labour and domestic work in private houses. The report also names Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza as places where children are sex-trafficked, and says children are exploited by foreign offenders as well as local ones.

The people it describes doing this are brokers and foster families, not strangers. That detail is the mechanism. A broker offers a job or schooling in a tourist economy a day's travel away, and a foster family provides the respectable arrangement that explains why a child is living in someone else's house in another part of the country. Both have lawful custody for everyday purposes, so the child is not missing, has no reason to be looked for, and in a domestic job is behind a door no inspector opens.

The report says the government did not adequately address corruption and official complicity, which is the part that determines whether any of this is interrupted. It gives no count of victims, and there is no Tanzanian court case or national inquiry in the sources behind this map.

So the account above exists because a foreign ministry writes a yearly report, using what embassies and organisations can see from outside. Tanzania teaches what that kind of record can and cannot do: it can name the practice and the towns, and it cannot name the number, the accused or the outcome. When an exploitation story turns on fostering or a job offer, ask who placed the child, what was promised to the family, and whether anyone has ever visited the house.

SEN.mechanism: Gold-mining camps pull in cash, migrant men and recruited girls at once, and the only numbers for Senegal come from a foreign report because no survey of children here has ever been done.
SEN.story:
Kedougou, in Senegal's south-east, is gold country. Informal mining draws thousands of men to camps that appear where the ore is, pay in cash and are not registered anywhere, which is the setting the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report describes: organised networks transporting Nigerian women and girls, with victims in Kedougou as young as 12, into sex trafficking around the mines. The same networks move people on to mining regions in Mali, Burkina Faso and Cote d'Ivoire.

Several things about a mining camp make it work for the people running this. The buyers arrive with money and no families; the camps move when the digging moves, so no one builds a school, a clinic or a police post beside them; and the girls are foreign, brought across a border by the same network that controls where they sleep, so they have no one to go to and often no papers.

What is not known about Senegal is larger than what is. The Childlight research programme, which pools representative national surveys to estimate how many children are exploited online, reported in 2026 that it had such surveys for only 60 countries and that West and Central Africa provided none. A representative survey asks a random sample of young people what has happened to them, which is the only method that reaches abuse nobody reported at the time. Without one, the figure for children in Senegal exploited through phones and the internet is not low; it does not exist.

Senegal shows a problem described by outsiders in the places where outsiders can see it, which are the mines. When you see one region of a country named again and again in trafficking reports, ask whether that is where the exploitation is concentrated or where it is observable, and whether anyone has ever surveyed children anywhere else.

MYS.mechanism: Malaysia's role is storage: the files sit on servers rented in the country while the people who made them, sell them and watch them are somewhere else, and the same five per cent share returns every year.
MYS.story:
In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British organisation that searches for child sexual abuse material and asks hosting companies to delete it, acted on 17,046 web addresses whose files sat on servers in Malaysia. That was five per cent of everything it dealt with that year, the same share as in 2024.

Hosting is worth understanding plainly, because it is easy to misread. A website is files on a rented computer in a data centre. Whoever rents it can be anywhere, pay by card or cryptocurrency, upload from another continent and sell access to people in a third country. So a hosting figure tells you where the material is kept, not where the children in it live, not who abused them and not who is paying. The country appears on the list because its data centres are cheap, fast and willing, and because the Foundation found the files and sent a notice.

The notice is the other half of the mechanism. This body cannot take anything down itself; it identifies material and relies on the company to act. A share that stays the same two years running suggests the removals are happening one address at a time without anything changing about who is allowed to rent space and what checks they face.

There is no Malaysian court case or inquiry in the sources behind this map to say who runs these servers or who pays them. Malaysia shows that a large number can describe an infrastructure problem rather than a crime scene. When a country keeps appearing on hosting lists, ask which companies own the machines, how fast they delete material once told, and whether any law requires them to do it or penalises them for not.

CIV.mechanism: Cote d'Ivoire's place on this map is an absence of measurement: the global estimates of online child exploitation are built from surveys that have never been run anywhere in its region.
CIV.story:
There is no case, inquiry or court record for Cote d'Ivoire in the sources behind this map. The reason is worth more than a blank space, because it explains how every figure elsewhere on the map was made.

Most child sexual abuse is never reported to anyone with a file. Police records therefore count reporting, not abuse, and they vary with how easy and safe reporting is. The way around this is a representative survey: ask a randomly chosen sample of young people, in private, what has happened to them, and scale the answers to the population. That produces an estimate including the cases no official ever heard about.

The Childlight research programme pools such surveys to estimate how many children are exploited through phones and the internet. Its 2026 update rests on representative surveys from 60 countries, and West and Central Africa supplied none of them. For Cote d'Ivoire there is consequently no estimate at all, not a small one.

This has an effect on the world totals, not only on this country. A global figure assembled from the places that have surveys describes those places; the rest is covered by assumption or left out of the sum. The same is true of the other main sources. The UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries but only 72 supplied data for 2023, and in 2025, 14 per cent of the 23.4 million reports to the US tipline for online abuse could not be assigned to any country at all.

Cote d'Ivoire teaches how to read a quiet country on any map of this kind. Before concluding that a place has little of a problem, find out which measuring instrument would have detected it there, and whether that instrument has ever been used.

MRT.mechanism: Mauritania is unmeasured in both ways that matter: no survey has asked its children anything, and nothing in the record shows what reaches its police, so the country reads as quiet.
MRT.story:
Two different kinds of number lie behind any statement about child abuse in a country, and Mauritania has neither.

The first kind is administrative: cases that reached a police station, a prosecutor, a hospital or a child protection office. These exist only where someone reported and someone else wrote it down, so they rise when a country makes reporting easier and fall when people stop expecting anything to come of it. They are a record of institutions, read as a record of children.

The second kind comes from a representative survey, in which a random sample of young people is asked directly, in private, what has happened to them, and the answers are scaled up to the whole population. This is the only way to count what was never reported. The Childlight research programme, which pools these surveys to estimate online exploitation of children, reported in 2026 that it had them for 60 countries and that West and Central Africa had none.

So for Mauritania there is no survey estimate, and there is no case, inquiry or court record in the sources behind this map either. The honest description of the country's position is that nobody has looked in a way that would produce a number, which is not the same as a low number and cannot be used as one.

A survey costs money and requires permission, trained interviewers and a government willing to publish what comes back. Those three conditions, rather than the level of abuse, decide which countries have figures. When a country shows nothing, ask who would have to fund a survey there, who would have to approve it, and what they would have to agree to publish.

BHR.mechanism: Bahrain's figure depends entirely on what officials chose to record, because the survey method that catches unreported abuse has never been used anywhere in its region.
BHR.story:
Imagine trying to say how many children in a country have been groomed, blackmailed or filmed online using only the cases officials wrote down. You would be measuring four things at once: how many children were harmed, how many understood what had happened to them, how many had somewhere safe to say it, and how willing the office receiving it was to record it. Change any of the last three and the number moves without the abuse changing at all.

For Bahrain, that is the only kind of number available. There is no case, inquiry or court record in the sources behind this map, and the method that gets past official records has not been applied in the region. The Childlight research programme builds its estimates from representative surveys, in which a random sample of young people is asked in confidence what has happened to them; its 2026 update covers 60 countries, and the Middle East and North Africa supplied none.

The absence is regional rather than particular to Bahrain, which matters when the map is read as a comparison. Several neighbouring countries are blank for the same reason, so the contrast between them and a country with detailed figures is a contrast between research programmes, not between childhoods.

What this country teaches is to ask what a reported figure is a measure of before comparing it with another one. If a survey has never been run, the only honest statement is that the size of the problem is unknown, and the next question is whether a survey has been proposed, by whom, and whether its findings would be published.

BTN.mechanism: The map's estimates come from surveys that depend on money, permission and privacy, and nobody in South Asia has run one, so Bhutan has no figure to show.
BTN.story:
A number on a map like this one usually began as a conversation with a teenager. The method that produces estimates of online child sexual exploitation is a representative survey: a random sample of young people, chosen so that their answers can stand for the whole age group, asked what has actually happened to them and promised confidentiality.

Each of those conditions is a practical obstacle. Someone has to pay for the survey. A government has to permit researchers to ask children about sexual abuse and accept that the results will be published. And the child has to be able to answer in private, which is difficult when the questioning happens at home or in a classroom, and when the person asking might be known to the family.

The Childlight research programme, which pools these surveys into global estimates, reported in 2026 that it had representative data from 60 countries and none from South Asia. For Bhutan there is accordingly no estimate, and no case, inquiry or court record in the sources behind this map.

Bhutan's entry is really a lesson about the instrument. When a country has no figure, the question is not what its children are spared, but which of the three conditions failed: nobody funded the work, nobody permitted it, or no child could safely answer. Each has a different remedy, and each can be asked about by name.

PRK.mechanism: North Korea's near-zero count measures access to American internet services, not the safety of its children, because the reporting system that produces the world's figures only sees what US companies can see.
PRK.story:
In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children recorded 12 reports concerning North Korea. Set against the 23.4 million reports it received that year, the number looks like good news and is nothing of the kind.

The system behind it works in one direction. American technology companies are required by US law to report child sexual abuse material found on their services to this centre, which passes the information to police in the relevant country. Nearly every large reporting platform is American, so the figures describe what happens on American apps. A country's count rises with the number of its people using Facebook, Instagram, Google or Snapchat, and with how hard those companies look.

North Korea's population has almost no access to the global internet. There is nearly nothing for an American platform to detect, so almost nothing is reported, and the centre itself treats the 12 reports as a near-total absence of data rather than a measurement. No other source on this map fills the space, and the country has no national survey, inquiry or published court record in those sources.

The same bias shapes the whole dataset in a smaller way. A country whose people are heavily online with US services can appear to have a severe problem because it is visible, while a country disconnected from those services appears to have none.

North Korea is the clearest case of a number that describes the instrument instead of the subject. Whenever you see a count of online abuse reports by country, ask who is obliged to report, whose services they run, and how many people in that country could be using them.
